big_idea: We test predictions by collecting data from TWO populations and comparing.
learning_intention: We are learning to test a prediction by comparing two populations.
student_learning_goal: I can test a prediction by comparing two populations.
success_criteria: I can COLLECT data from two groups.
I can COMPARE the two groups.
I can EXPLAIN if my prediction was right.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Lucky Lou and Maybe Mae — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Class A and Class B fake data sets

minds_on.hook: Lucky Lou: Imagine TWO classes. Class A loves hockey. Class B loves soccer. PREDICT — same favourite? TEST! Lucky+Mae open: 'Class A, Class B — same math, different DATA!' Yesterday Mae predicted; today we compare TWO classes' data.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lucky Lou puppet in green. 'Detective friends — today we test predictions across TWO POPULATIONS.'

Define. 'A POPULATION is a GROUP we collect data from. Class A is one population. Class B is another.'

Demo. 'Predict — will Class A and Class B have the SAME favourite sport?'

Class A data (Grade 3 in Toronto): hockey 8, soccer 4, basketball 3, swim 2.
Class B data (Grade 3 in Vancouver): soccer 6, hockey 5, swim 4, basketball 2.

'Class A favourite: hockey. Class B favourite: soccer. Same? NO!'

'Lucky Lou says — predictions about populations might be RIGHT or WRONG. We TEST by collecting from BOTH.'

Now show three more comparisons:
- Class A pets vs Class B pets — likely DIFFERENT.
- Class A bedtime vs Class B bedtime — likely SAME.
- Class A breakfast vs Class B breakfast — likely SAME.

'Lucky Lou says — sometimes populations agree. Sometimes they don't. The TEST tells us.'

Explain the activity. Each pair gets a Two-Population Chart + 2 fake data sets. They:
1. Predict (same or different).
2. Compare data.
3. Decide if prediction was right.

'Lucky Lou says — every PREDICTION needs a TEST.'

steps.instruction: Hand out 4 two-population data sets. Pairs predict same/different.
Compare data and decide if prediction was right.
Stretch: explain WHY same or different.
Help with comparison technique — find favourite of each.

STRATEGY INVENT: Pairs decide HOW they will compare — by favourite only, by top 2, or by all rows. Two pairs share. Class debates which is most thorough. Cite Lehrer & Schauble (2002) — distribution-level comparison is research-target.
steps.teacher_prompt: Lucky: 'Different comparison strategies. The MATH says: more rows = more truth.'

differentiation.for_movement_learners: Walk between two stations. NO-PAPER VERSION: teacher reads two class tallies aloud; children stand for matches, sit for differences. Body becomes the comparison.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Five signals: prediction; collection; comparison; decision; explanation.

consolidation.exit_routine: Lucky+Mae two-population refrain — 'Class A, Class B — same math, different DATA!' (3x). Each child compares one value across both populations.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child compares ONE population only — repairing the single-group trap at Grade 3
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On two-population comparison, the trap is favourite-only comparison: child compares only the most-frequent value, missing the distribution. Lehrer & Schauble (2002) and Konold & Pollatsek (2002) frame distribution-aware comparison as the Grade-3 data target.

Yesterday Mae predicted from data. Today comparing two populations. Lesson 4 mean/mode; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Two-population activity. Child writes only Class A's favourite.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Lucky Lou asks — what about Class B?'

Guide. 'Look at BOTH columns. Class A favourite? Class B favourite? Same?'

Generalise. 'Lucky Lou says — D2.2 means TEST across TWO populations. ONE doesn't test.'

If still single: split chart. 'Cover Class A. Look at Class B. Now compare.'
common_misconceptions: One population = test. (Repair: D2.2 needs TWO.)
Same data = same population. (Repair: groups differ.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child names Class A favourite but freezes at B: side-by-side both surveys; child names BOTH favourites first.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child compares only top values: drill 'compare ALL rows — count similarities and differences.'
DIAGNOSTIC C — child compares but cannot decide: force the sentence frame 'Class A and Class B are ___ because ___.'

parts_outline.task: Predict for 4 scenarios: same or different favourite.
Look at 2 data sets and identify each population's favourite.
Decide: was the prediction right? Why?
